fields.h1: Build User Provisioning Automation That Opens Accounts by Role
fields.hero_description: Build user provisioning automation that opens, changes, and closes app accounts by role, and logs every change.
fields.features_heading: What Your Provisioning App Takes Off IT
fields.features_subheading: Each person gets the accounts their role calls for, and each change to those accounts lands in one log.
fields.feature_1:
A role list that decides who gets what

The app keeps a table of roles, the apps each role gets, and the access level in each app. Change a row by prompting, and the next person hired into that role gets the new set.
fields.feature_2:
Accounts created through each app's API

The app reads new hires and role changes from your HR system. It then calls the user API of each tool on the role list, such as team chat or the CRM, to open or change an account.
fields.feature_3:
Admin rights wait for the app owner

Accounts with admin or billing rights wait for the owner of that app, who gets a Slack or email alert to approve or decline. Standard accounts on the role list open without a wait.
fields.feature_4:
A log row for every account change

Each account opened, changed, or closed is saved as a row: the person, the app, the access level, the rule that fired, and the time. The log sits in a database you own.
fields.feature_5:
A live board of pending and failed changes

IT sees every change that is waiting for an approval or that an app rejected. The board updates live as each app answers, and a failed call stays on top until someone retries it.
fields.feature_6:
The provisioning app's code in GitHub

Export the app's full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Your security team can read every rule that opens or closes an account, and review changes like any other code.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Moments When Access Has to Change
fields.tab_content_1:
Four accounts open before a support agent's first day

The HR system marks Odalys Fenwick as a new support agent at Brindlecove Insurance, starting Monday. The support agent role gets 4 apps: email, team chat, the help desk, and the phone system. The app opens all 4 accounts before her first day and sends her manager, Tobias Elmgren, a direct message that lists them.
fields.tab_content_2:
Sales to finance: 2 apps added and 1 removed

Ruairi Castellanos moves from sales to finance at Pellworth Freight. On the day of the move, the app adds the 2 apps the finance role gets: the ledger and the expense tool. His CRM seat stays open for 7 days while he hands over his deals, and then the app removes it.
fields.tab_content_3:
Without an extension, all 3 contractor accounts close

Imani Okafor designs catalog pages for Fernmoor Outdoor on a contract that ends in 14 days, and she has accounts in 3 apps. Seven days before the end date, her manager, Linnea Hartwell, gets an email with an Extend button. If Linnea does not extend the contract, the app closes all 3 accounts on the end date.
fields.tab_content_4:
IT hears which of 6 accounts failed to close

HR records Friday as Bartholomew Szeto's last day at Quillfield Dental. At the end of that day, the app closes his accounts in 6 apps, and 5 of the 6 confirm. The scheduling system returns an error. The IT lead, Ines Varga, gets a direct message that names the 1 account still open.

fields.howto_title: How to Build User Provisioning Automation
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to map each role to its apps and build user provisioning automation that keeps every account matched to a role.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List every app and its owner
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Mark the accounts that need approval
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down every app you pay for, the person who owns each one, and how an account gets created in it today. Mark the apps that hold customer or payroll data, because those accounts need the closest watch.
fields.howto_step_2_des: For each role, name the apps it gets and the level of access in each, such as viewer, editor, or admin. Start with the 5 roles you hire into most often, and leave rare roles as manual requests for now.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose one system whose records drive every account change, such as your HR system. Every account change then follows a change to that record, and nobody opens accounts from a chat request.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Mark each app and access level that should wait for a person, such as admin rights or billing. Name an approver for each one, and decide how long a request can wait before their manager hears about it.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Describe the role list, the trigger, and the approval rules in one prompt. Emergent writes the app and the IT board that tracks it, and you change any rule later by prompting instead of editing a script.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Connect the HR system and each app
fields.howto_step_6_des: Connect the HR system and every app on the role list through its API. For each app, find the admin API it documents for creating and closing users, and put any app without one on a manual list for IT.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Run one past hire, one team move, and one departure through the app against test accounts. Compare the accounts it opens and closes with what IT did by hand, and fix the role list before you switch it on.

faq_plan.a: User provisioning automation is software that keeps a person's app accounts in step with their HR record. It opens accounts for a new hire and closes them after a last day, and a move to another team swaps one set of apps for another. A role list decides which apps and access levels each person gets, and every change is logged.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up user provisioning automation?
faq_plan.a: Start with a role list that names the apps and access level for every role. Pick the HR record that triggers changes, mark which accounts need an approver, and describe all of it to Emergent's AI automation builder. Connect each app's API, then replay a past hire and a past departure against test accounts before you switch it on.

faq_plan.q: Is there a standard protocol for user provisioning automation?
faq_plan.a: Yes, SCIM. RFC 7644 defines SCIM as an application-level HTTP-based protocol for provisioning and managing identity data on the web. A client creates and updates users through it and removes an account with a DELETE request. For a tool with no SCIM endpoint, the app calls that tool's own user API instead.

faq_plan.q: What should trigger user provisioning automation for a new hire?
faq_plan.a: Use a change to the HR record, such as a status of hired with a start date, rather than an offer accepted by email. The start date gives the app a deadline to open accounts before day one. If you run recruitment automation, the accepted candidate it passes to HR can create that record.

faq_plan.q: Should user provisioning automation run on each change or on a schedule?
faq_plan.a: Run it on each change to the HR record, and add a nightly check on top. The change-driven run opens and closes accounts the day the HR record changes. The nightly check compares each app's user list with the role list and reports any account nobody expected, such as one an admin created by hand.

faq_plan.q: How do I decide which apps each role gets in user provisioning automation?
faq_plan.a: Give each role only the apps and access levels its work needs. NIST defines least privilege as restricting the access privileges of users to the minimum necessary to accomplish assigned tasks. Build each role's list from what people in that role open in a normal week, and send anything else through a request with an approver.

faq_plan.q: Can user provisioning automation create accounts for clients as well as employees?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The same pattern works for customer portal accounts: a signed contract triggers the account, and the client's plan sets what they can see. If you already run a client onboarding workflow, its last step can create the client's portal login. Emergent builds that app from a plain-English prompt and connects it to any tool with an API.

faq_plan.q: How does user provisioning automation keep access correct over time?
faq_plan.a: Run an access review every quarter. The app sends each app owner a list of who has an account and at what level, and the owner confirms or removes each one. Every answer is saved with the date and the reviewer in a database you own, and next quarter's review starts from it.

faq_plan.q: Do I need an identity provider for user provisioning automation?
faq_plan.a: No. The app can call each tool's own user API where the tool offers one, and a team with a dozen such apps can start there. If you already run an identity provider, connect it through its API and leave it the accounts it manages today. Emergent builds the provisioning app from a prompt, and the free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: How do I grant temporary access with user provisioning automation?
faq_plan.a: Give every access request outside the role list an end date. The person asks through a form, the app's owner approves, and the app removes the access on that date and logs it. A support agent who needs the refund tool for a week of escalations gets 7 days. If you run customer service automation, link the escalated ticket to the request so the owner sees why.

plan.angle: The top 10 are vendor glossaries and identity-suite blogs that define provisioning and list benefits without showing a single account change. This page treats user provisioning automation as a role list plus four account moments: a new hire's role opens its apps, a move between teams adds and removes apps, a contractor's accounts close on the contract end date, and a departure closes every account with IT told about any that fails. The FAQ covers deactivate versus delete, the trigger, SCIM, role design, client accounts, access reviews, identity providers and temporary access, and leaves onboarding tasks and exit checklists to the employee onboarding and offboarding pages.

findings.issue: The source scope is dropped (rework-checklist item 2). Okta's page says this of SCIM apps only: 'If an admin deprovisions a user's profile inside Okta, the user resource inside your SCIM app is updated with active=false'. Without 'SCIM', the sentence covers every Okta provisioning integration. The source does not support that, and the plan's SCIM coverage never reaches the copy. Naming Okta as an example implies no partnership, which is fine.
findings.fix: In Okta's SCIM provisioning, for example, deprovisioning a user in Okta updates that user's account in the connected SCIM app with active=false.
